study.name: Memory Beliefs Drive the Memory Bias on Value-based Decisions
study.citation: Mechera-Ostrovsky, T., & Gluth, S. (2018). Memory beliefs drive the memory bias on value-based decisions. Scientific Reports, 8, 10592. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-28728-9
study.description: Preregistered remember-and-decide study with 48 Swiss supermarket snacks; data and analysis scripts at https://osf.io/ze8xh/.

description: Wanting to eat: participants reported "their willingness to eat each snack at the end of the experiment on a continuous rating scale from 0 (=not at all) to 10 (=very much)"; after a first pass they saw every snack again with its initial rating and could adjust it, and were incentivized (two snacks drawn, the higher-rated one given). The adjusted rating (preference_mat2, the value the authors analysed) is imported; the RA compilation had used the first pass. All 91 participants in the OSF archive (the paper analysed 64 after exclusions). Stimulus key: the source stores snack ids 1-48 only. The authors' analysis script (Data_Analysis_SubjectiveBelief.R, OSF) maps every id to the three-letter abbreviation participants learned and typed during cued recall ("e.g., sni for Snickers", paper); the same map is recovered from all 91 participants' typed recall answers. Ids run in blocks of 8 matching the lab's six categories (bars, bonbons, chocolate, wine gums, nuts, salty snacks), and participants' salty/sweet key presses at encoding follow those blocks. 23 snacks are named because the lab's own 2018 study files name that product (OSF qrv2e, CDdata G.id); the other 25 keep dataset-scoped codes ostroglu-<abbreviation> (see quality_note). snack_to_item.json carries the per-id evidence.
quality_note: 25 of 48 items are dataset-scoped codes 'ostroglu-<abbreviation>': the three-letter abbreviation participants learned for each snack (documented by the authors' analysis script), whose product no surviving document names. Likely readings, not asserted: kag = Kaegi fret; kar = unknown bar; cou = possibly Kinder Country; bal = Balisto; fru = fruit drops?; car = caramels?; chu = Chupa Chups; cor = unknown chocolate; tru = truffles?; tor = probably Torino (Camille Bloch); cho = a chocolate (typed "lin" 8 times: Lindt?); exc = Lindt Excellence; red = unknown wine gum; loo = unknown wine gum; him = probably Himbeeren (raspberry gums); stu = Studentenfutter (trail mix); erd = Erdnuesse (peanuts); nus = probably a nut mix; man = Mandeln (almonds); mex = unknown nut snack; chi = chips (typed "tor" 22 times: tortilla chips?); fli = Flips (peanut puffs); kam = Kambly (typed "gol" 26 times: Goldfischli crackers?); pop = popcorn; rol = salty snack (typed "sal" 6 times). The other 23 items are named from the lab's own snack list (OSF qrv2e).
